source.title: Convergent Representations of Linguistic Constructions in Human and Artificial Neural Systems
source.authors: Pegah Ramezani; T. Kinfe; Andreas K. Maier; Achim Schilling; Patrick Krauss

record.file_problem: The full paper text is present. The text has minor extraction artifacts and inconsistent participant counts: the abstract says 10, Methods says 12, and the group-level results report n=11.
record.tranche_reason: The study extends prior computational findings about argument-structure constructions to human EEG and evaluates whether the reported timing and pairwise pattern appear in human neural responses. It does not test the listed scale, cross-modal, seed, mapping, feature, metric-dependence, or shared-cause versions directly.
record.gate_note: The study reports human EEG construction classification and describes its qualitative resemblance to results from earlier language-model studies. Those earlier model results are cited, not measured here; this paper does not measure representational distances between models, compare them across scale or capability, or quantify human–model representational alignment. EEG classification results are recorded as related findings under fits_no_version. Cited computational results are not rows.
record.test_reason: The study records only human EEG and decodes construction type from it. It runs no models and measures no model-to-model or human-to-model representational alignment. Its convergence claim is a qualitative comparison with the authors' earlier LSTM and BERT studies, which are cited, not re-measured. It invokes the Platonic representation idea only as an interpretation. The record's 'tests'/T3 contradicts its own finding that no version is tested, so it is corrected to discusses/T6.
record.authors_conclusion: Largely correct. The authors conclude that EEG carries construction-specific information, mostly at object positions and in the alpha band. They say the timing and pairwise similarity pattern qualitatively mirror their own prior recurrent and transformer model studies. They read this as consistent with convergence toward a 'Platonic' representational space. The comparison with models is qualitative and not measured in this paper.
record.recipe_differences: The study uses EEG feature analysis and SVM decoding of human sentence responses; it does not reproduce a model-representation similarity method from the cited convergence sources.
record.method_sensitivity: Construction pair and sentence position changed the observed discriminability: effects were strongest at object positions, while some pairwise contrasts were not above chance. The study also reports differing sensitivity across frequency bands and feature types.

fits_no_version.finding: Human EEG decodes some argument-structure construction pairs above chance at object-aligned epochs (e.g. Ditransitive vs Resultative 0.705 vs permutation 0.456). Others do not differ from chance (Caused Motion vs Resultative 0.454; Ditransitive vs Transitive 0.471). Four-way decoding reached 30% against 25% chance.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Human EEG distinguishes some argument-structure constructions, mainly at late sentence positions, with graded pairwise separability.

fits_no_version.finding: Leave-verb-out cross-validation slightly lowered accuracy but kept the pairwise pattern; no numbers are given.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: EEG construction decoding is not fully explained by verb overlap between training and test sets.

fits_no_version.finding: The authors claim the EEG timing and pairwise similarity structure qualitatively mirror their earlier LSTM and BERT findings. They report no quantitative brain-model similarity.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Brains and language models show qualitatively similar construction-representation geometry (brain-model convergence).

record.problems: The study reports a small dataset: 12 participants recorded, with group-level decoding results for n=11, and 200 sentences. It acknowledges uncontrolled sentence length and lexical content. Several reported controls and figure results lack numerical values, and the participant count differs across the abstract, Methods, and results.
record.rows_left_out: No additional numerical human EEG classification results bearing on the related construction-discrimination finding were omitted. The paper's feature-count plots and verb-controlled Figure 10 do not provide further numerical values in the text; the qualitative verb-controlled outcome is recorded in R8. Results attributed to prior language-model studies were excluded because they are cited rather than measured here.

untested.parts: No models of varying scale or capability, and no cross-model alignment measure.
No vision or language models and no paired image-caption data.
No networks trained from different seeds.
No mapping, stitching or relative-representation test between models or between brain and model.
No cross-model comparison of features, neurons or circuits.
No comparison of similarity metrics or input distributions for alignment.
No quantified alignment, so no measure of its completeness, plateau or causes.

record.verdict_notes: The participant count is inconsistent: the abstract says 10, Methods says 12, and Table 3 says n=11. A Wilcoxon W of 66 matches n=11. The rows are correctly unlinked (['none']). The paper cites the Platonic Representation Hypothesis only as an interpretive frame.

versions.untested_parts: No model-size or capability sweep, nor comparison of independently trained models with different architectures, objectives, or data.
No paired image-caption data or vision–language models.
No comparison of networks trained from different initializations or analysis of shared features or subspaces across seeds.
No representation mapping, stitching, relative-representation, or unpaired alignment test.
No cross-model comparison of interpretable features, neurons, or circuits.
No comparison of representation-similarity metrics, their settings, or input distributions.
No direct measurement of model-to-model alignment, its plateau or completeness, or the causal contribution of shared data or objectives.
